name: Nighthawks
kicker: Edward Hopper’s 1942 painting · A late-night diner and American loneliness
briefing: Edward Hopper painted this diner scene in 1942, just after the attack on Pearl Harbor, when blacked-out windows made American cities feel lonelier than ever. Inside, three customers sit under cold fluorescent light while a white-uniformed counterman works behind the counter — and famously, there is no door for anyone to walk through. It hangs today in the Art Institute of Chicago, one of the most reproduced and parodied paintings in American art.

tossups.p: A 1984 parody of this painting by Gottfried Helnwein, titled _Boulevard of Broken Dreams_, swaps in Hollywood icons like Marilyn Monroe and Elvis Presley. Critics often link this painting to Ernest Hemingway’s short story “The Killers.”
tossups.r: A cash register sits in the window of a shop across the street from the diner shown here. For 10 points, name this painting of an all-night diner by Edward Hopper.

tossups.p: The artist’s wife, Jo, is believed to have modeled for the red-dressed woman in this painting, as she did for most of the female figures in her husband’s work. The building across the street, with its half-drawn window shades, echoes one in the same artist’s _Early Sunday Morning_.
tossups.r: A sign across the top of the diner in this painting advertises Phillies cigars for five cents. For 10 points, name this painting of a late-night diner by Edward Hopper.

tossups.p: This painting is sometimes said to be set at an oddly angled corner the artist noticed in Greenwich Village, though no exact real-life diner has ever been confirmed. Its two male customers wear dark fedoras, and some retell a story that the painting’s title comes from the beak-like nose of the man seated beside the woman in red.
tossups.r: Painted in 1942, just weeks after Pearl Harbor, this work now hangs in the Art Institute of Chicago. For 10 points, name this painting of a diner at night by Edward Hopper.

tossups.p: Two large silver coffee urns sit behind the counter in this painting, which the Art Institute of Chicago bought the same year it was completed. A counterman in a white uniform crouches behind that counter, seemingly the only person in the scene who is actually working.
tossups.r: Viewers have long noted that this painting’s diner has no visible door for anyone to enter. For 10 points, name this painting of three customers at an all-night diner, by Edward Hopper.

tossups.p: Sharp diagonal lines and almost no visible brushstrokes give this painting an eerily cool, photographic stillness. A sign advertising five-cent Phillies cigars runs across the top of the diner, whose customers sit behind a curving, wraparound window.
tossups.r: Painted right after the attack on Pearl Harbor, this work shows an empty city street outside a brightly lit diner. For 10 points, name this painting, Edward Hopper’s most famous.

tossups.p: Gottfried Helnwein’s parody of this painting, _Boulevard of Broken Dreams_, replaces its four figures with Marilyn Monroe, Elvis Presley, and other classic Hollywood stars. The diner inside this painting has no visible door, a detail many critics connect to its theme of isolation.
tossups.r: Two men in fedoras and a woman in a red dress sit at the counter in this painting. For 10 points, name this 1942 painting of a late-night diner by Edward Hopper.

tossups.p: One popular story claims this painting’s title comes from the hawk-like profile of the man seated beside the woman in red. A cash register sits in a shop window across the street from the diner shown here.
tossups.r: This painting now hangs in the Art Institute of Chicago, which purchased it not long after it was painted. For 10 points, name this Edward Hopper painting of an all-night diner.

tossups.p: Critics often compare this painting to a Hemingway short story about two hitmen waiting in a diner. The building across its street resembles one from the same artist’s _Early Sunday Morning_, and his wife Jo modeled for its one female figure.
tossups.r: A sign in this painting advertises Phillies cigars for a nickel. For 10 points, name this Edward Hopper painting showing three late-night customers at a diner counter.

tossups.p: Two silver canisters sit behind the counter in this painting, completed just weeks after the bombing of Pearl Harbor in December 1941. Its diner, unlike a real one, was painted with no visible door for customers to use.
tossups.r: A woman in a red dress and two men in fedoras sit at the counter in this painting. For 10 points, name this painting of an empty city street and a brightly lit diner, by Edward Hopper.

tossups.p: Gottfried Helnwein restaged this painting as _Boulevard of Broken Dreams_, placing Marilyn Monroe and Elvis Presley at the same counter shown here. The scene may be based on a restaurant the artist spotted on an oddly angled corner in Greenwich Village.
tossups.r: This painting hangs today in the Art Institute of Chicago. For 10 points, name this Edward Hopper painting of three customers at a late-night diner.

tossups.p: A white-uniformed counterman bends over behind the counter in this painting, the only figure shown doing any work. Critics have compared this painting’s eerie calm to a scene from a Hemingway short story about two gunmen waiting in a diner.
tossups.r: This painting’s diner advertises Phillies cigars for five cents on a sign across its top. For 10 points, name this painting of a late-night diner by Edward Hopper.

tossups.p: This painting has no visible door leading into its diner, a choice many art historians read as reinforcing its mood of isolation. A building with a darkened, half-shaded window stands across the empty street from that diner, echoing a similar building in the same artist’s _Early Sunday Morning_.
tossups.r: The painter’s wife, Jo, modeled for the red-dressed woman seated here. For 10 points, name this Edward Hopper painting of three customers at a diner counter at night.

tossups.p: Two large coffee urns gleam behind the counter in this painting, completed in 1942 not long after the United States entered World War II. A parody of this painting called _Boulevard of Broken Dreams_ later replaced its figures with Marilyn Monroe, Elvis Presley, and other stars.
tossups.r: This painting’s diner has no door that viewers can see. For 10 points, name this painting of a brightly lit, all-night diner by Edward Hopper.

tossups.p: This painting’s two male customers wear dark fedoras while its one woman wears a red dress, and all three sit under cold fluorescent light that spills out onto an otherwise empty street. The Art Institute of Chicago bought this painting the same year it was finished.
tossups.r: Painted shortly after Pearl Harbor, this work shows an all-night diner seen through a wraparound window. For 10 points, name this Edward Hopper painting.

trap.title: The painting, not Hopper
trap.body: Nearly every clue describes details inside the painting, and the giveaway nearly always ends “…by Edward Hopper,” which tempts a fast buzz with the artist’s name instead of the title. Two other paintings turn up in real tossups too: Gottfried Helnwein’s parody _Boulevard of Broken Dreams_, which swaps in Marilyn Monroe and Elvis Presley, and Hopper’s own _Early Sunday Morning_, a completely different painting.
trap.fix: Listen for “this painting” or “this work” — that phrasing wants the title _Nighthawks_, not Edward Hopper, and not one of the other paintings mentioned along the way.
